uncited: Wavelet and Transform-based Compression reduces volumetric data size by projecting the signal into a frequency or residual domain where energy is compacted, allowing for efficient quantization and entropy coding [S1].
It solves the problem of high memory bandwidth and storage requirements for large 3D datasets by exploiting spatial correlation and smoothness [S1].

What sets it apart from [Value compression](6-value-compression.md), which operates directly on amplitude statistics, and [Sparse structures](5-sparse-structures.md), which address geometric sparsity, is its reliance on linear basis functions (wavelets, pyramids) to decorrelate data, enabling multi-resolution access and superior handling of smooth gradients [S1][S5].
All methods in this family share the mechanism of decomposing the input volume $V$ into a set of coefficients $C$ using a linear transform, followed by encoding and optional decoding for rendering.
**Transform:** The volume is decomposed using a separable 1D filter bank applied along each axis.
For a 3D volume, this results in subbands representing different frequency components.
In wavelet transforms, these are typically approximation (low-pass) and detail (high-pass) coefficients.
In Laplacian pyramids, they are detail residuals between levels of a Gaussian pyramid.
The approximation subband from level $j$ is further decomposed at level $j+1$, creating a tree-like structure of coefficients.
This allows for multi-resolution access, where coarse data is available at the root and fine details are deeper in the tree.
**Quantization and Entropy Encoding:** Coefficients are quantized (lossy) or kept precise (lossless).
Entropy coding (e.g., Huffman, Arithmetic, Run-Length) is applied to the quantized or raw coefficients to produce the compressed bitstream.
**Reconstruction:** To render, the necessary coefficients are decoded and the inverse transform is applied.
This can be done globally (full reconstruction) or locally (block-wise or point-wise) to support adaptive resolution rendering.
The application of wavelet transforms to volumetric data originated in the mid-1990s as a generalization of 2D image compression techniques.
Early work by researchers such as Sweldens and Pierrakos explored the use of lifting schemes and separable 3D wavelets for medical imaging [S1].

The method became standard in scientific visualization for its ability to provide lossless compression with high ratios for smooth data, and lossy compression with minimal visual artifacts for ray-marched volumes.
It is widely used in medical imaging (DICOM), climate data archives, and real-time volume rendering systems that require level-of-detail (LOD) streaming.
